opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a bit of a framing trick, honestly. When people say a vision-language-action model only needs a few hundred demonstrations to learn a new task, that's true at the fine-tuning stage, but it hides where the data actually went. The backbone was trained on billions of image-text pairs scraped from the internet, and on top of that you usually have a large cross-embodiment robot dataset collected over months or years by many labs. So it's not little data. It's a lot of data spent upfront, and then you amortize it.

That said, I don't think the framing is entirely wrong, because amortization is exactly the point. If the expensive part is paid once and every new task or robot afterward is cheap, then from the point of view of someone deploying a robot it really does feel like a little-data approach. The question is what the pretraining is actually buying you. The internet data gives you semantics really well: what a mug is, what "put the red block next to the bowl" means, some common-sense scene understanding. What it doesn't give you is physics, contact, or the low-level motor skills. Nobody on the internet labels torques. So for the actual control part you're still pretty data-hungry, and that's where the teleoperation bottleneck comes back.

That's also why I'm biased toward simulation for the control side. For locomotion, and increasingly for whole-body control, you can generate essentially unlimited experience in sim with reinforcement learning, massively parallel on GPUs, and the robot learns behaviors no human could easily demonstrate, like recovering from a fall or walking on rough terrain. So the way I see it, the realistic picture isn't little data versus big data. It's different sources of big data for different layers: internet-scale data for understanding and high-level reasoning, simulation for robust low-level skills, and a comparatively small amount of real-world data to glue them together and close the gap. Calling the whole thing little data mostly reflects which part of the pipeline you happen to be looking at.

r001.rationale: The response says the approach is not really little-data once pretraining is counted, citing billions of internet image-text pairs and large robot datasets collected over months or years.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think "little data" is a bit of a misnomer, or at least it depends on where you draw the boundary. If you look only at the robot-specific part, sure, you might be fine-tuning on a few hundred demonstrations, or in some cases doing zero-shot prompting, so from the robotics lab's point of view it feels very data-efficient. But the model you're standing on has consumed essentially the entire internet of images and text. All of that data is still there, you've just moved the cost somewhere else and paid it once up front.

So I'd frame it more as a transfer approach than a little-data approach. The question that actually matters is how much of what the model learned from web data is relevant to the robot's problem. For semantics, for recognizing objects, understanding instructions, reasoning about what a scene is, a lot of it transfers, and that's genuinely useful. For the low-level control part, the thing I spend most of my time on, the internet is almost silent. There are no YouTube videos that tell you what joint torques to apply when a quadruped slips on gravel. That information has to come from somewhere, and in our case it comes from simulation, where we can generate what is effectively unlimited experience very cheaply.

So I actually see the two things as complementary rather than competing. The VLM gives you a high-level understanding that would be very expensive to learn from scratch on a robot, and simulation plus reinforcement learning gives you the physical competence that web data can't provide. Neither one is little data. They're both enormous amounts of data, just coming from different sources that happen to be cheap. And honestly, I'd rather we talk about it that way, because when people hear "little data" they expect the method to work in regimes where it fundamentally can't yet, and then they're disappointed when the robot falls over.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the pretrained model has consumed essentially the entire internet of images and text, so counting that pretraining makes the approach data-intensive despite using few robot-specific demonstrations.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be careful about what you mean by “little data.” If you’re using a pretrained vision-language model, there’s already a huge amount of data behind that model. So I wouldn’t call the whole approach data-efficient just because you only collected a small number of robot demonstrations.

But there is a meaningful distinction: how much robot-specific data do you need to get a new task working? Robot data is expensive to collect, and if pretraining lets you reuse knowledge from images and text, that can be very useful. You’re transferring some of the learning burden to data that’s easier to obtain.

The question is how much of that knowledge actually transfers to control. Recognizing an object or understanding an instruction doesn’t automatically tell you how to interact with it physically. So I’d describe it as potentially requiring little additional robot data, rather than little data overall.

r001.rationale: The response says a pretrained vision-language model already has a huge amount of data behind it, so the approach is not data-efficient overall when that pretraining data is counted.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you count as data. If you count all the data that went into pretraining the vision-language model, then clearly it’s not a little-data approach. There’s a huge amount of information already in that model.

But from the perspective of somebody trying to get a robot to do a particular task, the question is how much additional robot data you need. Can you take those pretrained representations and learn a useful controller from a small number of demonstrations? In that sense, it can be a little-data approach, because you’re transferring knowledge instead of learning everything from scratch.

The caveat is that understanding an image or a language instruction doesn’t automatically give you the ability to control a robot. You still have to learn how actions affect the world. So I’d distinguish between having a lot of prior knowledge and needing little task-specific interaction data.

r001.rationale: It says counting all data used to pretrain the vision-language model means it is not a little-data approach, because the model contains a huge amount of information.
